questions.q: Which of these correctly lists the six policy lifecycle stages in order, per this lesson?
options: Drafting, review, approval, publication, review and revision, retirement
Publication, retirement, drafting, approval, review, revision
Approval, drafting, retirement, review, publication, revision
Retirement, drafting, publication, review, approval, revision
questions.explain: The lifecycle runs drafting through review, approval, publication, scheduled review/revision, and finally retirement.

questions.q: At the drafting stage, who typically authors the first controlled version of a policy?
options: A steward, with the owner identifying the business need
An external regulator
A random employee with no connection to the domain
Nobody — policies appear fully formed with no drafting stage
questions.explain: The owner identifies the need and assigns an author — typically a steward — consistent with Lesson 19's owner/steward division of labor.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say publishing a policy 'nobody can find' is barely different from not publishing it at all?
options: A policy only has real effect if the people expected to follow it can actually access it
Publication is a purely ceremonial stage with no real-world purpose
Policies are automatically emailed to every employee the moment they're drafted
Publication and retirement are the exact same stage
questions.explain: The point of publication is making the approved policy reach its intended audience — if nobody can find it, it functions as if unpublished.

questions.q: According to this lesson, which stage of the policy lifecycle do organizations tend to handle worst?
options: Retirement
Drafting
Approval
Publication
questions.explain: It's easy to stop paying attention to an old policy, but much harder to formally retire it — leaving obsolete rules indistinguishable from current ones.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT listed as something that can trigger a policy's review and revision?
options: A competitor publishing an unrelated marketing campaign
The scheduled review date arriving
A regulatory change making part of the policy outdated
A business change, like a merger, making the policy's scope wrong
questions.explain: Real triggers are the scheduled date, regulatory change, business change, or a steward/committee flag — an unrelated competitor campaign isn't one of them.
